stem: A 17-year-old boy has fever and shortness of breath 2 months after an allogeneic stem cell transplant for leukemia. He takes immunosuppressive drugs. His blood neutrophil count is within the reference range. Examination shows diffuse crackles and chest imaging shows an interstitial pneumonia. Lung biopsy shows enlarged cells with large intranuclear inclusions surrounded by a clear halo.
oneliner: 17M + 2 months after allogeneic stem cell transplant on immunosuppressants + normal neutrophil count + fever, dyspnea, diffuse crackles + interstitial pneumonia + owl-eye intranuclear inclusions → which function is decreased?
ask: Decrease in which immune function most likely allowed this infection?

options.B: Eosinophil killing of helminth larvae in tissue
options.C: Mast cell degranulation after IgE cross-linking
options.D: Dendritic cell migration to the lymph nodes
options.E: Cytotoxic T-cell killing of infected cells

whyNot.A: His **neutrophil count is normal**, and neutrophil defects give **pyogenic bacterial** infections, not the **viral inclusions** seen here
whyNot.B: Eosinophils handle **helminths**; nothing in the stem suggests a parasite
whyNot.C: Mast cells drive **immediate hypersensitivity**; no allergy features here
whyNot.D: The **immunosuppressive drugs** he takes act on T cells, and the biopsy shows **virus-infected cells** that only cytotoxic T cells clear

answer: Cytotoxic T-cell killing of infected cells (cell-mediated immunity)
why: **Owl-eye intranuclear inclusions** mean **cytomegalovirus**. After transplant, immunosuppressants **blunt T-cell immunity**, the main defence against herpesviruses, so latent CMV reactivates and causes **interstitial pneumonitis**.
chain: Latent CMV escapes control and reactivates

idea.rule: Loss of cell-mediated immunity lets latent intracellular and herpesvirus infections reactivate.
also: HIV with low CD4: CMV retinitis, Pneumocystis, toxoplasmosis
Transplant recipients: BK virus, EBV lymphoproliferation
Glucocorticoids and calcineurin inhibitors: reactivated VZV
DiGeorge syndrome: recurrent viral and fungal infections

stem: A 30-year-old woman is followed with serial tests after exposure to an infectious agent. For the first 3 days she is well. Virus titer then rises, peaks at day 5 and is undetectable by day 14. Symptoms start at day 4, peak at day 6 and resolve by day 10. Antibody appears at day 7 and stays elevated for years.
oneliner: 30F + well for 3 days, then symptoms peak day 6 and resolve by day 10 + virus undetectable by day 14 + antibody persists for years → which disorder fits the course?
ask: Which of the following best fits this clinical course?

whyNot.A: **HIV** persists for years and is never cleared; here the virus is **undetectable by day 14**
whyNot.C: **SSPE** appears **years after measles** as slow progressive neurologic decline
whyNot.D: **CJD** is a prion disease with no antibody response and relentless decline
whyNot.E: **GBS** is a neuropathy that begins **after** an infection has cleared; here symptoms peak alongside the rising virus titer

why: A short asymptomatic incubation, a **peak then complete resolution** and **virus cleared** as antibody rises is an **acute self-limited infection**. Persistent and slow infections do not clear or follow years-long courses.
chain: Titer falls to zero, symptoms resolve

idea.rule: Acute viral disease: incubation, peak, clearance; persistent and slow infections break that pattern.
also: Persistent: HIV, hepatitis B and C chronic infection
Prion: CJD, with no immune clearance
